notes:
I've written notes for all 13 verses, but some of what you asked for is missing. I didn't reach any of the Catholic or Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), netbible.org's own notes, bibleodyssey.org, any Lutheran site, or any page on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on Micah 2, so those parts are left out. Where Church Fathers or rabbis appear below, it's only because Protestant commentaries quote them. I sorted traditions by commentator: Calvin and Poole for Reformed, Gill and Spurgeon for Baptist, Wesley for Methodist, and Guzik and Chuck Smith for the Pentecostal/charismatic slot (both are actually Calvary Chapel).

**Overview**
- The chapter falls into three parts. Verses 1–5 are judgment on the rich who exploit the poor. Verses 6–11 are an argument between false prophets (perhaps speaking for the land-grabbers) and Micah. Verses 12–13 suddenly offer hope for a remnant. Patterson summarizes Micah 2 - It contains three oracles... The first message pronounces divine judgment against the wealthy oppressors of the middle class and poor (Micah 2:1–5). The second message is a dispute between the false prophets (perhaps representing wealthy land-grabbers trying to silence Micah) and Micah, God's true prophet (Micah 2:6–11). The third message shifts abruptly... to a word of hope — https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_2_commentary

**v. 1**
- Guzik: all sin is bad, but sin planned in advance is worse. The real test of faithfulness is whether we stay faithful when we have the power to sin. Guzik also suggests "morning light" may point to the law courts, which opened at dawn, so the corruption was legal. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-2/
- Calvin: Micah addresses Judah as well as the northern kingdom. The sins here break the "second table" of the Ten Commandments (duties to neighbour), not idolatry. The Prophet does not here speak only against the Israelites... but he... addresses also the Jews. He refers not here to idolatry, as in the last chapter; but inveighs against sins condemned in the second table. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/micah-2.html
- Gill: the "iniquity" could include idolatry, impurity or coveting. The night hours should be spent meditating on God's goodness and examining one's heart. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-1.htm
- Benson: "in the power of their hand" means nobody could stop them. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-1.htm
- Wesley (Methodist): Because they can; without regarding right or wrong. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-micah/

**v. 2**
- Keil & Delitzsch: the word "covet" points back to the commandment against coveting. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-1.htm
- Poole, Gill and Pusey (via Barnes) all compare this to Ahab taking Naboth's vineyard. Pusey quotes an early Christian writer who applies the verse to Christ's enemies plotting by night to seize "the inheritance". — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-2.htm
- Wesley: family land was not supposed to be sold permanently, in a case where God hath forbidden them to sell their heritage. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-micah/
- Coffman: the Jubilee laws were being ignored. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/micah-2.html
- Background: Excavations at eighth-century sites such as Tel Lachish and Tel Beersheba reveal sudden increases in large storage jars, indicative of grain accumulation by wealthy landowners. — https://biblehub.com/micah/2.htm

**v. 3**
- The punishment matches the sin: they "devised" evil, so God "devises" disaster. they devised, now God will devise (Poole), and Poole names the Assyrian power as the means. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/micah/2.htm
- Guzik makes the same point. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-2/
- Wesley, on "walk haughtily": You have made others hang the head; so shall you now. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-micah/

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: the same words will be both Israel's lament and the enemy's mockery. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-4.htm
- Who are the "traitors"? The Pulpit Commentary says the Assyrian or Babylonian king, as a rebel against God. Keil says God hands the land to the heathen. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-4.htm
- Poole offers several readings of "turning away": God turning from them, or the enemy dividing the fields. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/micah/2.htm

**v. 5**
- Calvin links "dividing by lot" to the original allotment of the land and to its periodic restoration at Jubilee. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/micah-2.html
- MacKay: Because of their sin the LORD will no longer recognize them as his, and they will have no portion in the restored land. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_2_commentary
- Wesley: They shall no more be the congregation of the Lord, nor their children after them. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-micah/

**v. 6**
- Guzik: the people dismissed God's word as mere "prattle", so God stopped sending prophets. Micah preached 16–25 years before anyone responded under Hezekiah. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-2/
- Calvin: this shows the arrogance of ungodly people trying to silence God's prophets, as though they themselves were doubly and treble prophets. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/micah-2.html
- Wesley: So God doth in his displeasure grant their desire. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-micah/

**v. 7** (traditions apply this verse differently)
- Who is speaking is unclear. Some take the first half as the false prophets claiming such judgments could never come from their God. The NIV makes it Micah's own question (MacKay). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_2_commentary
- Pusey (via Barnes): the people thought God would have to change to reject them. Micah answers, "not God is changed, but you." God's promise was to Jacob, not to those who were but named Jacob — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-7.htm
- Calvin (Reformed): the people blamed God's word for their own wickedness. God's words are good to the upright, because through them we learn of his love. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/micah-2.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist) applies the verse to preaching and revival. Human commands cannot silence the Spirit, and believers wrongly treat Him as "straitened" (limited) when they expect only small blessings. — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/is-the-spirit-of-the-lord-straitened (Guzik quotes the same line: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-2/)
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel): the people wanted to dictate to the Spirit and silence Him. He also applies this against scholars who belittle Scripture. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Mic/Mic_1.cfm
- Wesley: God's power and kindness are no less than before. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-micah/
- Modern textual note: the Pulpit Commentary reports S.R. Driver's suggestion that changing one vowel gives "Is the ear of the Lord shortened?" — https://biblehub.com/micah/2-7.htm
- The Douay-Rheims (Catholic) translation makes the first half the words of the house of Jacob: "The house of Jacob saith…" — https://biblehub.com/micah/2-7.htm

**v. 8**
- Poole: they had rebelled long ago and lately added fresh violence. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/micah/2.htm
- Wesley sees conflict on every level: Israel against Judah, subjects against kings, the great against the poor. They stripped people who were going about their business fearing nothing. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-micah/
- One reading is that the victims were returning soldiers who should have been honoured. — https://biblehub.com/micah/2.htm

**v. 9**
- Wesley takes "the women" as widows, whom the law protected. "My glory" is God's generosity, the children's inheritance. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-micah/
- Calvin: cruelty even to women and children showed that their boast of being God's chosen people was empty. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/micah-2.html
- Pulpit Commentary: "forever" means the oppressors never repented or made restitution. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/micah-2.html

**v. 10**
- Wesley and Poole: the land was given as a "rest", but only on condition of obedience. Defiled by sin, the land will "spue you out". — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-micah/ and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/micah/2.htm
- Guzik reads it as exposing the false prophets: they can never give real rest. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-2/

**v. 11**
- Calvin: true prophets were "men of the Spirit" who passed on only what God gave them. Israel wanted flattery, they desired to be deceived by false adulation to their own ruin. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/micah-2.html
- Guzik: the false prophets, not Micah, were the real "prattlers". — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-2/
- Pulpit Commentary: a preacher who never interferes with people's pleasures will always be popular. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/micah-2.html

**v. 12** (real disagreement here)
- Most read this as a promise of restoration. Guzik says the remnant would be many. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-2/
- Wesley: fulfilled in part, when the Jews returned out of Babylon, but more fully when Christ by his gospel gathered together in one, all the children of God — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-micah/
- Pusey (via Barnes): the return from Babylon didn't fit "all Jacob". Fulfilment began with Jewish believers gathered into the Church. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-12.htm
- Calvin (Reformed) disagrees with the majority. He grants that most interpreters see a promise about Christ's kingdom. But he concludes that the passage, taken in context with chapter 3, bears evidently the appearance of a commination (a threat): God gathers the people only to scatter them. — https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_jonah_micah_nahum/micah_2_12-13.htm
- Benson also reports this "siege" reading: the people crammed into Samaria and Jerusalem to be besieged. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-12.htm
- Poole records a further view: verse 12 is the false prophet's flattering speech, and Micah answers it in verse 13. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/micah/2.htm
- Keil rejects that view, since a false prophet would not speak as God ("I will gather"). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-12.htm
- Dispensational view (preceptaustin): the remnant will be gathered at Bozrah, besieged by the forces of the Antichrist, and fulfilment is still future. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/micah_2_commentary

**v. 13** ("the Breaker")
- Christ as the Breaker:
  - Guzik: a messianic title of Jesus, the trailblazer at the front of His flock. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-2/
  - Gill (Baptist): "best to interpret" as Christ himself. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/micah/2-13.html
  - MacLaren: the words have their only real accomplishment in the office and working of Jesus Christ. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/micah/christ-the-breaker.cfm
  - Matthew Henry: Bishop Pearson applied it to Christ's resurrection, breaking out of the grave. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/micah/2-13.html
- Pulpit Commentary: "clearly Messianic", and not a description of the siege of Samaria or Jerusalem. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-13.htm
- Keil: a second Moses, meaning Zerubbabel, and in the highest sense Christ. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-13.htm
- Poole, by contrast, records that some took the Breaker to be Shalmaneser's Assyrian army. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/micah/2-13.htm
- Hawker notes that Poole and Trapp are among the older commentators who don't identify the Breaker as the Messiah. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/christ_the_breaker
- Wesley's note mixes the two: "the door of escape out of their captivity", but also no city so strong that the Assyrians won't enter it. — https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-micah/
- Jewish readings (as reported by Protestant writers):
  - Rabbinic tradition makes the Breaker Elijah and the King the Messiah. Rashi says the Breaker is the people's saviour clearing a path. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/christ_the_breaker
  - Pocock and Henry connect this with John the Baptist as forerunner. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mic/Mic_002.cfm
  - Ellicott (citing Pearson) says Jewish sources took "the Breaker" as a title of the Messiah. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/micah-2.html
